Asia Society Mourns Passing of President Emeritus Nicholas Platt, 1936-2026

July 28, 2026 — Asia Society mourns the passing of Ambassador Nicholas Platt, who served as the organization’s fifth President from 1992 to 2004, and who dedicated most of his distinguished career to U.S.-Asia and U.S.-China relations. 

Ambassador Platt’s illustrious 34-years in the U.S. Foreign Service placed him at the center of one of the twentieth century’s most consequential diplomatic turns: the normalization of relations between the United States and China. He also served as U.S. Ambassador to Zambia (1982-1984), the Philippines (1987-1991), and Pakistan (1991-1992).

His involvement with Asia began as a student of Chinese language in Taiwan in the early 1960s, following his graduation from Harvard College in 1957 and from Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies, where he received his MA in 1959. His early Foreign Service assignments included postings in Hong Kong (1964-68), Beijing (1973-74), and Tokyo (1974-77). 

He was one of the original “China Boys,” young Foreign Service officers who trained in Mandarin when China was closed to the West and who formed the advance team for President Richard Nixon’s historic 1972 visit to Beijing that signaled the resumption of relations between the United States and China. As Nixon departed China, he told the young diplomat, “You China boys will have lots to do from now on,” a line Platt later took as the title of his 2010 memoir, China Boys: How U.S. Relations with the PRC Began and Grew.

He was one of the first members of the U.S. Liaison Office in Beijing when the United States established a mission there in 1973. Amb. Platt’s government service in Washington, D.C. included positions as China analyst, Director of Japanese Affairs, National Security Council Staff Member for Asian Affairs, Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense (responsible for politico-military relations with Japan, Korea, China, and Southeast Asia), Acting Assistant Secretary of State for UN Affairs (1981-1982), and Executive Secretary of the Department of State (1985-1987).

On his retirement from government service in 1992, Ambassador Platt joined Asia Society serving as President until 2004, leading the organization through a momentous chapter of its history and guiding the organization through extraordinary growth to address key developments in Asia and U.S.-Asia relations. 

Asia Society underwent a dramatic expansion during the 1990s and early 2000s. At the time, Ambassador Platt noted, “The tides of war, economic growth, trade, technology, investment, and immigration have placed Asia and Asians in the middle of American life. The Asia Society is uniquely positioned to bring Asians, Americans, and Asian Americans together with each other through its programs and networking opportunities.” 

Ambassador Platt championed Asia Society’s cultural and performing arts programming, seeing the arts as a vital means of fostering dialogue and deepening understanding between the peoples of Asia and the United States. During his tenure, Asia Society strengthened its role as a public cultural institution. He oversaw dramatic growth of the Museum’s exhibition and public spaces culminating in the 2001 renovation and expansion of its Park Avenue headquarters, doubling the art exhibition spaces and adding performance and conference facilities along with a café and expanded retail operation. He fostered the growth of arts and exhibitions programming to bring further emphasis on contemporary Asian and Asian American artists. 

During his tenure, Asia Society drew a steady stream of top Asian and U.S. foreign policy figures to speak on issues of the day, while track II diplomacy efforts allowed for the examination of issues related to China and Taiwan, India and Pakistan, Iran, and more. 

Asia Society’s reach outside New York City grew significantly during Ambassador Platt's presidency. Under his leadership, the organization's Education program expanded substantially with the establishment of the Asian Educational Resource Center (AERC), a major initiative focused on improving teaching about Asia in U.S. K-12 schools. The department also initiated a program offering resources to support internationally-themed high schools serving low-income and minority students.

The opening of an office in San Francisco complemented existing U.S. centers, while in Asia, he led the opening of new centers in Australia and the Philippines, and laid the groundwork for the establishment of permanent campuses for Asia Society in Hong Kong and Houston. At the same time, he saw the potential of technology to transform communication, and expanded the Society’s institutional communications efforts with the launch of the organization’s first online presence and robust digital content development. 

In 2000, the launch in New York of a program series on Asian social issues brought attention to less-covered challenges and leaders from Asia in the areas of women’s rights, HIV/AIDS, and the environment, seeking areas of common ground between Asia and the United States. These efforts drew enthusiastic new audiences to Asia Society while laying the groundwork for the organization’s ongoing efforts in the areas of health and the environment. 

In the wake of 9/11, Ambassador Platt marshaled various disciplines and resources across Asia Society to assess root causes and responses in Asia, while positioning the organization to respond to the need for information about Afghanistan and Pakistan.

After stepping down as President, Ambassador Platt remained an enthusiastic and engaged supporter of the organization, speaking frequently at programs, attending events, and offering wise counsel. He was beloved by staff, who fondly remember his diplomacy in action as a transformational leader and mentor, and for his warmth and sense of humor, and graciousness.
